title: Functional Massage Versus Passive Mobilization After Total Knee Replacement
official: Functional Recovery in the Acute Phase After Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Two Different Physiotherapy Protocols
summary:
This study compares two physiotherapy treatments to help adults recover movement after total knee replacement: functional massage and passive knee mobilization. The main question is whether functional massage helps patients bend their knee further by the time they leave the acute hospital ward.

Forty adults undergoing replacement of one knee or both knees during the same operation will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group will receive functional massage according to Olaf Evjenth, and the other will receive passive manual knee mobilization. Both groups will also receive the same standard rehabilitation and pain management.

The assigned treatment will be provided once daily, starting on the first day after surgery and continuing until hospital discharge. Each treatment will last 10 minutes per operated knee.

A clinician who does not know which treatment the patient received will assess knee movement. The study will also evaluate pain, functional mobility, patient-reported outcomes, and length of hospital stay.

interventions.name: Functional Massage According to Olaf Evjenth

criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Male and female patients aged 18 to 79 years.
* Scheduled for elective primary total knee arthroplasty, either unilateral or simultaneous bilateral.
* Ability to understand the nature of the study and provide written informed consent.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Revision total knee arthroplasty.
* Age 80 years or older.
* Severe comorbidities that could interfere with participation in the rehabilitation protocol or outcome assessment, including severe heart failure, severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe obesity with body mass index greater than 40 kg/m², or neurological conditions with significant motor deficits.
* Cognitive deficits that prevent understanding and signing the informed consent or active participation in rehabilitation.
* Total knee arthroplasty performed for non-degenerative causes, such as acute trauma or tumors.
* Concomitant participation in another interventional clinical trial.
